claim: A homozygous missense mutation c.616C>T in the YME1L1 gene was identified in four affected children of a consanguineous Saudi Arabian family.
source: We identified a homozygous mutation in the nuclear encoded mitochondrial escape 1-like 1 gene YME1L1, member of the AAA protease family, as a cause of a novel mitochondriopathy in a consanguineous pedigree of Saudi Arabian descent.
evidence: The manuscript reports whole exome sequencing results identifying the mutation, confirmed by Sanger sequencing, with segregation analysis in the family.

claim: The YME1L1 mutation c.616C>T causes an amino acid substitution p.R149W in the mitochondrial targeting sequence.
source: The YME1L1 gene mutation c.616C>T causes the exchange of highly conserved hydrophilic arginine to hydrophobic tryptophan (p.R149W, NP_055078) within the N-terminal MTS (Figure 1E–G).
evidence: The mutation location and amino acid change are documented through sequencing data and protein domain analysis shown in Figure 1E-G.

claim: All four affected patients presented with intellectual disability, motor developmental delay, expressive speech delay, optic nerve atrophy, visual impairment, and hearing impairment.
source: All four patients presented with intellectual disability, motor developmental delay, expressive speech delay, optic nerve atrophy associated with visual impairment, hearing impairment, but no facial dysmorphism (Figure 1B, Table 1).
evidence: Clinical phenotyping data is presented in Table 1 and Figure 1B showing patient photographs.

claim: Cranial MRI revealed leukoencephalopathy in all four patients.
source: Cranial MRI revealed leukoencephalopathy in all patients and signs of brain atrophy in patients II.9 and II.11 (Figure 1C).
evidence: MRI images in Figure 1C show hyperintense changes indicative of leukoencephalopathy.

claim: Lactate levels and lactate/pyruvate ratios were elevated in blood and/or cerebrospinal fluid of three patients.
source: Lactate levels and lactate/pyruvate ratios were elevated in blood and/or cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) of three patients as indicators of a mitochondriopathy, while alanine levels were normal in blood and cerebrospinal fluid samples.
evidence: Biochemical measurements from patient samples are reported.

claim: Muscle biopsy from patient II.5 revealed mitochondria with altered cristae morphology ('parking lots') and paracristalline inclusions.
source: Analysis of a muscle biopsy specimen from patient II.5 revealed mitochondria with altered cristae morphology (so-called 'parking lots') and paracristalline inclusions as well as a neurogenic pattern with grouped fibers indicating denervation, but no conspicuous ragged red fibers in the Gomori trichrome staining (Figure 1D).
evidence: Electron microscopy and histological staining results are shown in Figure 1D.

claim: YME1L1 mRNA levels remain unaltered in patient fibroblasts compared to controls.
source: YME1L1R149W was below detection levels or profoundly reduced in patient whole cell lysates and in mitochondrial enriched fractions of patient fibroblasts, while mRNA levels remain unaltered (Figure 1H,I, Figure 1–source data 1, Figure 1–figure supplement 1).
evidence: qPCR data shown in Figure 1H demonstrates no significant difference in mRNA levels.

claim: YME1L1R149W protein levels are below detection or profoundly reduced in patient fibroblasts.
source: YME1L1R149W was below detection levels or profoundly reduced in patient whole cell lysates and in mitochondrial enriched fractions of patient fibroblasts, while mRNA levels remain unaltered (Figure 1H,I, Figure 1–source data 1, Figure 1–figure supplement 1).
evidence: Western blot analysis in Figure 1I shows reduced or absent YME1L1 protein.

claim: YME1L1R149W is targeted to mitochondria.
source: Both YME1L1 and YME1L1R149W co-localized with the mitochondrial marker protein ATPase subunit ß, demonstrating mitochondrial targeting of the mutant protein.
evidence: Immunofluorescence co-localization data shown in Figure 2A demonstrates mitochondrial localization.

claim: Inhibition of the proteasome does not stabilize YME1L1R149W.
source: Consistently, inhibition of the proteasome did not stabilize mutant YME1L1 (Figure 2B), suggesting that reduced levels of YME1L1R149W are not caused by proteasomal degradation of non-imported YME1L1 precursor proteins.
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 2B shows no stabilization of YME1L1R149W upon MG132 treatment.

claim: The R149W mutation abrogates MPP-mediated processing of YME1L1.
source: Mutation of arginine at position 149 abrogated MPP-mediated processing of YME1L1, suggesting that amino acid 151 forms the N-terminal amino acid of mature YME1L1.
evidence: Cell-free MPP cleavage assays shown in Figure 2C demonstrate loss of processing with R149W mutation.

claim: Replacement of arginine 149 by tryptophan abolished maturation of YME1L1 by MPP in vitro.
source: Replacement of arginine 149 by tryptophan similarly abolished maturation of YME1L1 by MPP in vitro (Figure 2D).
evidence: In vitro MPP cleavage assay results shown in Figure 2D demonstrate lack of processing.

claim: YME1L1 is a nuclear genome-encoded ATP-dependent metalloprotease embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: YME1L1, a member of the AAA family of ATPases (ATPases associated with a variety of cell activities), is a nuclear genome-encoded ATP-dependent metalloprotease embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane (IM), with its protease domain facing the intermembrane space (IMS) (also termed i-AAA protease) (Leonhard et al., 1996; Shah et al., 2000; Weber et al., 1996).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature establishing YME1L1 localization and function.

claim: YME1L1 import into mitochondria is accompanied by proteolytic processing via the mitochondrial processing peptidase (MPP).
source: Its import into mitochondria is accompanied by proteolytic processing via the mitochondrial processing peptidase (MPP), which cleaves off the mitochondrial targeting sequence (MTS) (Rainey et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rainey et al., 2006.

claim: The mature YME1L1 protein assembles into a homo-oligomeric complex within the inner mitochondrial membrane.
source: The mature protein assembles into a homo-oligomeric complex within the IM (Leonhard et al., 1996; Van Dyck and Langer, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: YME1L1 degrades intermembrane space and inner membrane proteins including PRELID1, protein translocase components, and OPA1.
source: YME1L1 degrades both IMS and IM proteins such as lipid transfer proteins (Potting et al., 2013), components of protein translocases of the IM (Baker et al., 2012; Rainbolt et al., 2015), and the dynamin-like GTPase optic atrophy 1 (OPA1) (Anand et al., 2014; Rainbolt et al., 2015; van der Bliek and Koehler, 2003).
evidence: Multiple citations support the substrate specificity of YME1L1.

claim: OPA1 is mutated in dominant optic atrophy.
source: The OPA1 gene (MIM*605290), mutated in dominant optic atrophy (Delettre et al., 2000), encodes a mediator of mitochondrial fusion that also orchestrates mitochondrial cristae morphogenesis (Cipolat et al., 2004; Frezza et al., 2006; Olichon et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Delettre et al., 2000.

claim: OPA1 is processed by two peptidases in the inner membrane: YME1L1 and OMA1.
source: OPA1 is processed by two peptidases in the IM, YME1L1 and OMA1 (overlapping with the m-AAA protease 1 homolog), which thereby balance fusion and fission of mitochondria (MacVicar and Langer, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to MacVicar and Langer, 2016.

claim: Long OPA1 forms (L-OPA1) carry out mitochondrial fusion.
source: Long OPA1 forms (L-OPA1) carry out mitochondrial fusion, while short forms (S-OPA1) are dispensable for fusion but contribute to mitochondrial fission when accumulated (Anand et al., 2014; Ehses et al., 2009; Griparic et al., 2007; Head et al., 2009; Song et al., 2007).
evidence: Multiple citations support the functional roles of different OPA1 forms.

claim: Loss of YME1L1 accelerates OMA1-dependent L-OPA1 cleavage, resulting in S-OPA1 accumulation and mitochondrial network fragmentation.
source: Loss of YME1L1 accelerates OMA1-dependent L-OPA1 cleavage, resulting in S-OPA1 accumulation, increased mitochondrial fission, and mitochondrial network fragmentation (Anand et al., 2014; Wai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Anand et al., 2014 and Wai et al., 2015.

claim: The dominant negative E381Q mutation in the ATPase domain of YME1L1 prevents degradation of YME1L1R149W.
source: However, by preventing the proteolytic activity of YME1L1 upon ectopic expression of the dominant-negative YME1L1E381Q, harboring a point mutation in the ATPase domain, we were able to stabilize not only the known YME1L1 substrate PRELID1 (Potting et al., 2013) but also observed accumulation of both the precursor and mature forms of YME1L1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3A shows stabilization of YME1L1 forms with E381Q mutation.

claim: YME1L1 mediates auto-catalytic degradation of mutant YME1L1R149W.
source: These results suggest that YME1L1 mediates degradation of mutant YME1L1R149W, which accumulates in the precursor form due to the mutation of the MPP cleavage site and thus is likely recognized as a misfolded protein in the IM.
evidence: This is inferred from the stabilization experiments with the E381Q mutation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: PRELID1 accumulated in patient II.5 fibroblasts compared to controls.
source: PRELID1, a lipid transfer protein for phosphatidic acid in the IMS, is constitutively degraded by YME1L1 (Potting et al., 2013). PRELID1 accumulated in primary human fibroblasts (HAF) of patient II.5 when compared to controls (Figure 3B), consistent with the low levels of YME1L1R149W present in mitochondria (Figure 1I, Figure 1–figure supplement 1).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3B shows increased PRELID1 levels in patient cells.

claim: An altered cleavage pattern of OPA1 was identified in patient cells.
source: We similarly identified an altered cleavage pattern of OPA1 in patient cells, albeit more modestly than in knockout mouse cells (Figure 3C).
evidence: Western blot analysis in Figure 3C shows altered OPA1 processing pattern.

claim: YME1L1R149W retains proteolytic activity.
source: This suggests that YME1L1R149W retains proteolytic activity.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of residual OPA1 processing in patient cells.

claim: YME1L1R149W assembles into protein complexes of approximately 2 MDa.
source: Similar to YME1L1, the mutant variants of YME1L1 were recovered in protein complexes of ~2 MDa (Figure 3D).
evidence: Sucrose gradient centrifugation data in Figure 3D shows complex formation.

claim: The R149W mutation does not impair the formation of the i-AAA protease complex.
source: Notably, we also observed assembly of the precursor form of YME1L1R149W/E381Q, demonstrating that the disease-causing mutation R149W does not impair the formation of the i-AAA protease complex.
evidence: Sucrose gradient data in Figure 3D shows assembly of mutant precursor forms.

claim: YME1L1R149W is a hypomorphic allele that retains partial YME1L1 activity.
source: Together, we conclude that YME1L1R149W is a hypomorphic allele that retains partial YME1L1 activity, which reconciles the embryonic lethality (Wai et al., 2015) of Yme1l1 knockout mice with the milder phenotype in our patients with a homozygous YME1L1 missense mutation.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observed residual function in patient cells and comparison with knockout mouse phenotype.

claim: Patient II.5 fibroblasts show increased mitochondrial network fragmentation compared to controls.
source: We detected an increase in shortened and fragmented mitochondrial networks in HAF of patient II.5 relative to a control (Figure 4A,B, Videos 1–4, Figure 4–source data 1), consistent with the more severe fragmentation phenotype in Yme1l1 KO mouse fibroblasts (Anand et al., 2014).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy and quantification in Figure 4A,B shows increased fragmentation.

claim: Human YME1L1 but not YME1L1R149W can complement mitochondrial fragmentation in Yme1l1-/- mouse fibroblasts.
source: We therefore transiently expressed human YME1L1R149W and YME1L1 in murine adult cardiac Yme1l1-/-fibroblasts (Wai et al., 2015) and observed that human YME1L1 but not YME1L1R149W was able to complement mitochondrial fragmentation.
evidence: Complementation experiments shown in Figure 4C,D demonstrate rescue by wild-type but not mutant YME1L1.

claim: YME1L1R149W can partially tubulate mitochondria in Yme1l1-/- mouse fibroblasts.
source: Of note, the human mutant variant was still able to partially tubulate mitochondria (Figure 4C,D, Figure 4–source data 1), consistent with the notion that YME1L1R149W retains residual function.
evidence: Microscopy data in Figure 4C,D shows partial rescue of mitochondrial morphology.

claim: Proliferation of patient II.5 fibroblasts is significantly reduced compared to healthy controls.
source: Proliferation of patient II.5 fibroblasts was significantly reduced compared to those of healthy controls, while the level of induced apoptotic cell death remained unaffected (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5–source data 1, Figure 5–source data 1, Figure 5–source data 1).
evidence: Cell viability and BrdU proliferation assays shown in Figure 5A,B demonstrate reduced proliferation.

claim: The level of induced apoptotic cell death remained unaffected in patient II.5 fibroblasts.
source: Proliferation of patient II.5 fibroblasts was significantly reduced compared to those of healthy controls, while the level of induced apoptotic cell death remained unaffected (Figure 5A–C, Figure 5–source data 1, Figure 5–source data 1, Figure 5–source data 1).
evidence: Cleaved PARP analysis shown in Figure 5C shows no difference in apoptosis.

claim: Respiratory chain enzymatic activities are within the normal physiological range in patient fibroblasts.
source: Analysis of the respiratory chain in patient fibroblasts revealed the specific enzymatic activities to be within the normal physiological range and subunit levels to be unaltered (Figure 5D,E), consistent with the observation in Yme1l1–depleted hearts (Wai et al., 2015).
evidence: Respiratory chain enzyme activity measurements shown in Figure 5D are within reference ranges.

claim: Respiratory chain subunit levels are unaltered in patient fibroblasts.
source: Analysis of the respiratory chain in patient fibroblasts revealed the specific enzymatic activities to be within the normal physiological range and subunit levels to be unaltered (Figure 5D,E), consistent with the observation in Yme1l1–depleted hearts (Wai et al., 2015).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 5E shows similar levels of COX4 and NDUFB6.

claim: Patient cells show reduced steady state levels of various mitochondrial compartment markers indicating a general reduction of mitochondrial mass.
source: However, the reduced steady state levels of various mitochondrial compartment markers in patient cells indicate a general reduction of mitochondrial mass in YME1L1R149W cells (Figure 5E, Figure 5F).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 5F shows decreased levels of TOMM20, Cytochrome c, SDHA, and Cyclophilin D.

claim: All four patients were born at term without complications and with normal anthropometric data.
source: Four affected children of healthy, consanguineous parents of Saudi Arabian descent were born at term without complications and with normal anthropometric data (Figure 1A).
evidence: Clinical history data is reported in the manuscript.

claim: Medical history gave no indication for perinatal brain damage as a cause for the reported patient phenotypes.
source: Medical history gave no indication for perinatal brain damage as a cause for the reported patient phenotypes.
evidence: Clinical history review is reported.

claim: Patients II.9 and II.11 had microcephaly.
source: Inconsistent features were microcephaly (II.9, II.11) or macrocephaly (II.5), ataxia (II.5, II.8, II.9), hyperkinesia (II.9), and athetotic and stereotypic movements (II.11).
evidence: Clinical phenotyping data is presented in Table 1.

claim: Patient II.5 had macrocephaly.
source: Inconsistent features were microcephaly (II.9, II.11) or macrocephaly (II.5), ataxia (II.5, II.8, II.9), hyperkinesia (II.9), and athetotic and stereotypic movements (II.11).
evidence: Clinical phenotyping data is presented in Table 1.

claim: Patients II.5, II.8, and II.9 had ataxia.
source: Inconsistent features were microcephaly (II.9, II.11) or macrocephaly (II.5), ataxia (II.5, II.8, II.9), hyperkinesia (II.9), and athetotic and stereotypic movements (II.11).
evidence: Clinical phenotyping data is presented in Table 1.

claim: Patient II.9 had hyperkinesia.
source: Inconsistent features were microcephaly (II.9, II.11) or macrocephaly (II.5), ataxia (II.5, II.8, II.9), hyperkinesia (II.9), and athetotic and stereotypic movements (II.11).
evidence: Clinical phenotyping data is presented in Table 1.

claim: Patient II.11 had athetotic and stereotypic movements.
source: Inconsistent features were microcephaly (II.9, II.11) or macrocephaly (II.5), ataxia (II.5, II.8, II.9), hyperkinesia (II.9), and athetotic and stereotypic movements (II.11).
evidence: Clinical phenotyping data is presented in Table 1.

claim: Patients II.9 and II.11 showed signs of brain atrophy on cranial MRI.
source: Cranial MRI revealed leukoencephalopathy in all patients and signs of brain atrophy in patients II.9 and II.11 (Figure 1C).
evidence: MRI images in Figure 1C show cerebral atrophy.

claim: Muscle biopsy from patient II.5 showed a neurogenic pattern with grouped fibers indicating denervation.
source: Analysis of a muscle biopsy specimen from patient II.5 revealed mitochondria with altered cristae morphology (so-called 'parking lots') and paracristalline inclusions as well as a neurogenic pattern with grouped fibers indicating denervation, but no conspicuous ragged red fibers in the Gomori trichrome staining (Figure 1D).
evidence: Histological analysis shown in Figure 1D demonstrates neurogenic pattern.

claim: Muscle biopsy from patient II.5 showed no conspicuous ragged red fibers in the Gomori trichrome staining.
source: Analysis of a muscle biopsy specimen from patient II.5 revealed mitochondria with altered cristae morphology (so-called 'parking lots') and paracristalline inclusions as well as a neurogenic pattern with grouped fibers indicating denervation, but no conspicuous ragged red fibers in the Gomori trichrome staining (Figure 1D).
evidence: Gomori trichrome staining shown in Figure 1D shows no ragged red fibers.

claim: Chromosome analysis, mitochondrial DNA sequencing, and genetic testing for fragile X syndrome, Nijmegen breakage syndrome, and ataxia teleangiectasia were normal.
source: Results of chromosome analysis, mitochondrial DNA sequencing and genetic testing for fragile X syndrome, Nijmegen breakage syndrome, and ataxia teleangiectasia were normal.
evidence: Genetic testing results are reported.

claim: Biochemical analyses gave no indication for adrenoleukodystrophy, GM1/GM2 gangliosidoses, Sandhoff disease, Tay-Sachs disease, Gaucher disease, Fabry disease, Krabbe disease, Mucopolysaccharidosis type IVB, neuronal ceroid-lipofuscinoses 1 and 2, and congenital disorder of glycosylation (CDG) syndrome.
source: Similarly, biochemical analyses gave no indication for adrenoleukodystrophy, GM1/GM2 gangliosidoses, Sandhoff disease, Tay-Sachs disease, Gaucher disease, Fabry disease, Krabbe disease, Mucopolysaccharidosis type IVB, neuronal ceroid-lipofuscinoses 1 and 2, and congenital disorder of glycosylation (CDG) syndrome (data not shown).
evidence: Biochemical testing results are reported.

claim: Whole exome sequencing discovered the homozygous mutation c.616C>T in exon 5 of the YME1L1 gene.
source: Whole exome sequencing discovered the homozygous mutation c.616C>T in exon 5 of the YME1L1 gene (NM_014263), localized at position 149 of the YME1L1 protein, and leading to an amino acid exchange of arginine to tryptophan in the mitochondrial targeting site (MTS; p.R149W, NP_055078).
evidence: WES results are reported and shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The mutation lies within a protein region highly conserved throughout different species.
source: The mutation lies within a protein region, highly conserved throughout different species.
evidence: Sequence alignment shown in Figure 1G demonstrates conservation.

claim: YME1L1 was first identified in yeast in a screen for gene products that elevate the rate of mitochondrial DNA migration to the nucleus.
source: YME1L1 was first identified in yeast, in a screen for gene products that elevate the rate of mitochondrial DNA migration to the nucleus (Campbell et al., 1994; Thorsness et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Campbell et al., 1994 and Thorsness et al., 1993.

claim: The lack of yme1 impairs respiratory growth of yeast.
source: The lack of yme1 impairs respiratory growth of yeast highlighting its important function in mitochondrial maintenance (Nakai et al., 1995; Pearce and Sherman, 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Nakai et al., 1995 and Pearce and Sherman, 1995.

claim: Yme1l1 knockout mice show embryonic lethality.
source: Together, we conclude that YME1L1R149W is a hypomorphic allele that retains partial YME1L1 activity, which reconciles the embryonic lethality (Wai et al., 2015) of Yme1l1 knockout mice with the milder phenotype in our patients with a homozygous YME1L1 missense mutation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wai et al., 2015.

claim: The homozygous c.616C>T missense mutation is compatible with life, likely owing to the residual function of YME1L1R149W.
source: In contrast to complete gene deletion in the mouse (Wai et al., 2015), the homozygous c.616C<T missense mutation is compatible with life, likely owing to the residual function of YME1L1R149W.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of patient phenotype with mouse knockout lethality and observed residual function.

claim: The missense mutation affects the MPP processing site and impairs YME1L1 maturation, leading to its rapid degradation.
source: We demonstrate that the missense mutation affects the MPP processing site and impairs YME1L1 maturation, leading to its rapid degradation.
evidence: This is demonstrated through MPP cleavage assays and protein stability experiments shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: YME1L1R149W leads to a proliferation defect.
source: We further show that the YME1L1R149W leads to a proliferation defect, abnormal OPA1 processing and mitochondrial fragmentation.
evidence: Proliferation assays shown in Figure 5A,B demonstrate reduced proliferation.

claim: YME1L1R149W leads to abnormal OPA1 processing.
source: We further show that the YME1L1R149W leads to a proliferation defect, abnormal OPA1 processing and mitochondrial fragmentation.
evidence: Western blot analysis in Figure 3C shows altered OPA1 processing.

claim: YME1L1R149W leads to mitochondrial fragmentation.
source: We further show that the YME1L1R149W leads to a proliferation defect, abnormal OPA1 processing and mitochondrial fragmentation.
evidence: Microscopy analysis in Figure 4A,B shows increased mitochondrial fragmentation.

claim: Fusion and fission of mitochondria are essential to preserve cellular functions.
source: Since fusion and fission of mitochondria are essential to preserve cellular functions, it is conceivable that defects in these processes, contribute to the patient phenotype in a cell-type specific manner.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about mitochondrial dynamics.

claim: Defects in mitochondrial fusion and fission may contribute to the patient phenotype in a cell-type specific manner.
source: Since fusion and fission of mitochondria are essential to preserve cellular functions, it is conceivable that defects in these processes, contribute to the patient phenotype in a cell-type specific manner.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observed mitochondrial fragmentation and known importance of mitochondrial dynamics.

claim: YME1L1 mutations reveal an important role of YME1L1 for the maintenance of mitochondrial morphology in humans.
source: With our findings, we reveal an important role of YME1L1 for the maintenance of mitochondrial morphology in humans and link a loss of YME1L1 function to disease.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observed mitochondrial fragmentation in patient cells.

claim: Loss of YME1L1 function is linked to disease.
source: With our findings, we reveal an important role of YME1L1 for the maintenance of mitochondrial morphology in humans and link a loss of YME1L1 function to disease.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the identification of disease-causing mutations in YME1L1.

claim: YME1L1 joins other members of the AAA family of ATPases that have been linked to neurologic disease, such as spastin (SPG4) and paraplegin (SPG7).
source: YME1L1 thereby joins other members of the AAA family of ATPases that have already been linked to neurologic disease, such as spastin (SPG4, MIM*6042779 and paraplegin (SPG7, MIM*602783) gene, and in the gene encoding the YME1L1 substrate optic atrophy 1 (OPA1, MIM*605290) (De Michele et al., 1998; Hazan et al., 1994; Nielsen et al., 1997; Warnecke et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies linking these genes to disease.

claim: Mutations in OPA1 have been linked to neurologic disease.
source: YME1L1 thereby joins other members of the AAA family of ATPases that have already been linked to neurologic disease, such as spastin (SPG4, MIM*6042779 and paraplegin (SPG7, MIM*602783) gene, and in the gene encoding the YME1L1 substrate optic atrophy 1 (OPA1, MIM*605290) (De Michele et al., 1998; Hazan et al., 1994; Nielsen et al., 1997; Warnecke et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Future studies on further patients are required to determine the full phenotype spectrum associated with YME1L1 gene mutations.
source: Future studies on further patients are required to determine the full phenotype spectrum associated with YME1L1 gene mutations.
evidence: This is a statement about the need for additional research.

claim: Homozygosity linkage intervals with LOD>2 and length >1 Mb were identified using the Affymetrix SNP array 6.0.
source: Homozygosity linkage intervals (chr10:24,333,063–49,978,774, LOD=2.533) with LOD>2 and length >1 Mb were identified using the Affymetrix SNP array 6.0.
evidence: This describes the genetic mapping methodology used.

claim: More than 94% of the exon-coding regions were covered by at least 20 folds in whole exome sequencing.
source: The output sequences amounted to 12 Gb and >94% of the exon-coding regions were covered by at least 20 folds.
evidence: This describes the quality metrics of the sequencing data.

claim: The absence of homozygous deleterious variants in YME1L1 was confirmed in multiple databases including ESP, ExAC, 1000 Genome, dbSNP138, and an in-house Middle East origin exome database.
source: We confirmed the absence of homozygous deleterious variants (missense, nonsense, frameshift, splice site change) in YME1L1 in the NHLBI Exome Sequencing Project (ESP, http://evs.gs.washington.edu/EVS/; ExAC 0.3 http://exac.broadinstitute.org/), the 1000 Genome database (http://www.1000genomes.org/), the dbSNP138 (http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/SNP/), and our in-house 898 Middle East origin exome database.
evidence: This describes the bioinformatic validation of the mutation's rarity.

claim: The raw sequencing data is available under the sequence reads archive (SDA) accession no. SRP073309.
source: The raw data is available under the sequence reads archive (SDA) accession no. SRP073309.
evidence: This provides data availability information.

claim: Sanger sequencing confirmed the mutation in the patients and established the genotype in other family members.
source: Sanger sequencing of the YME1L1 gene (NM_014263, GRCh 38.5) confirmed the mutation in the patients and established the genotype in the other family members and in additional families.
evidence: This describes the validation and segregation analysis methodology.

claim: Assembled YME1L1R149W precursor forms may explain the residual activity of YME1L1 in patient fibroblasts.
source: Thus, assembled YME1L1R149W precursor forms may explain the residual activity of YME1L1 in patient fibroblasts (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation of precursor assembly and residual OPA1 processing.

claim: Low levels of mature YME1L1R149W may maintain residual proteolytic activity in the patient system.
source: Alternatively, and not mutually exclusive, low levels of mature YME1L1R149W may maintain residual proteolytic activity in the patient system.
evidence: This is proposed as an alternative or additional explanation for residual activity.

claim: Unbalanced mitochondrial dynamics play a role in neurodegenerative diseases.
source: Given the role of unbalanced mitochondrial dynamics in neurodegenerative diseases (Burté et al., 2015) and the observed, impaired OPA1 processing, we focused our attention on mitochondrial morphology in patient fibroblasts.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Burté et al., 2015.

claim: Deletion of murine Yme1l1 leads to accelerated processing of L-OPA1 by OMA1.
source: Deletion of murine Yme1l1 leads to accelerated processing of L-OPA1 by OMA1 (Anand et al., 2014; Rainbolt et al., 2016) and drives mitochondrial fragmentation in vitro (Baker et al., 2014) and in vivo (Korwitz et al., 2016; Wai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Deletion of murine Yme1l1 drives mitochondrial fragmentation in vitro and in vivo.
source: Deletion of murine Yme1l1 leads to accelerated processing of L-OPA1 by OMA1 (Anand et al., 2014; Rainbolt et al., 2016) and drives mitochondrial fragmentation in vitro (Baker et al., 2014) and in vivo (Korwitz et al., 2016; Wai et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Baker et al., 2014; Korwitz et al., 2016; and Wai et al., 2015.

claim: PRELID1 is a lipid transfer protein for phosphatidic acid in the intermembrane space.
source: PRELID1, a lipid transfer protein for phosphatidic acid in the IMS, is constitutively degraded by YME1L1 (Potting et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Potting et al., 2013.

claim: PRELID1 is constitutively degraded by YME1L1.
source: PRELID1, a lipid transfer protein for phosphatidic acid in the IMS, is constitutively degraded by YME1L1 (Potting et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Potting et al., 2013.

claim: OPA1 encodes a mediator of mitochondrial fusion that also orchestrates mitochondrial cristae morphogenesis.
source: The OPA1 gene (MIM*605290), mutated in dominant optic atrophy (Delettre et al., 2000), encodes a mediator of mitochondrial fusion that also orchestrates mitochondrial cristae morphogenesis (Cipolat et al., 2004; Frezza et al., 2006; Olichon et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Cipolat et al., 2004; Frezza et al., 2006; and Olichon et al., 2003.

claim: Short OPA1 forms (S-OPA1) are dispensable for fusion but contribute to mitochondrial fission when accumulated.
source: Long OPA1 forms (L-OPA1) carry out mitochondrial fusion, while short forms (S-OPA1) are dispensable for fusion but contribute to mitochondrial fission when accumulated (Anand et al., 2014; Ehses et al., 2009; Griparic et al., 2007; Head et al., 2009; Song et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Arginine residues are known to function as MPP recognition and cleavage sites.
source: Since the identified human mutation affects an arginine and such residues are known to function as MPP recognition and cleavage sites (Niidome et al., 1994), we asked whether arginine 149 is part of the MPP cleavage site in YME1L1.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Niidome et al., 1994.

claim: Amino acid 151 forms the N-terminal amino acid of mature YME1L1.
source: Mutation of arginine at position 149 abrogated MPP-mediated processing of YME1L1, suggesting that amino acid 151 forms the N-terminal amino acid of mature YME1L1.
evidence: This is inferred from the MPP cleavage site mapping experiments shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The mature form of YME1L1 remained stable in cells harboring YME1L1E381Q upon incubation with cycloheximide.
source: The mature form of YME1L1 remained stable in cells harboring YME1L1E381Q upon further incubation in the presence of cycloheximide, while ectopic expression of the wild type variant resulted in significantly lower levels of YME1L1 and reduced stability (Figure 3A).
evidence: Cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 3A demonstrate protein stability.

claim: Ectopic expression of wild type YME1L1 resulted in significantly lower levels of YME1L1 and reduced stability compared to YME1L1E381Q.
source: The mature form of YME1L1 remained stable in cells harboring YME1L1E381Q upon further incubation in the presence of cycloheximide, while ectopic expression of the wild type variant resulted in significantly lower levels of YME1L1 and reduced stability (Figure 3A).
evidence: Cycloheximide chase experiments shown in Figure 3A demonstrate differential stability.

claim: Both mature YME1L1R149W/E381Q and larger forms with a similar size to the precursor form of YME1L1 accumulated in HEK293T cells expressing the double mutant.
source: Both mature YME1L1R149W/E381Q and larger forms with a similar size to the precursor form of YME1L1 accumulated in these cells.
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3A shows accumulation of multiple YME1L1 forms.

claim: Stabilization of the precursor form of YME1L1 may allow another peptidase to cleave YME1L1 resulting in the accumulation of slightly smaller forms.
source: Stabilization of the precursor form of YME1L1 in these cells may allow another peptidase to cleave YME1L1 resulting in the accumulation of slightly smaller forms of YME1L1.
evidence: This is speculated based on the observation of multiple YME1L1 forms in the double mutant.

claim: YME1L1R149W accumulates in the precursor form due to the mutation of the MPP cleavage site and is likely recognized as a misfolded protein in the inner membrane.
source: These results suggest that YME1L1 mediates degradation of mutant YME1L1R149W, which accumulates in the precursor form due to the mutation of the MPP cleavage site and thus is likely recognized as a misfolded protein in the IM.
evidence: This is inferred from the MPP cleavage defect and auto-catalytic degradation experiments.

claim: Degradation of YME1L1R149W may occur intramolecularly and/or by endogenous YME1L1 in wild type HEK293T cells.
source: As the mutant YME1L1 variants were expressed in wild type HEK293T cells, we cannot distinguish whether degradation of YME1L1R149W occurs intramolecularly and/or by endogenous YME1L1 under these experimental conditions.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation in distinguishing mechanisms in the experimental system.

claim: The lack of wild-type YME1L1 in patient cells with homozygous YME1L1 mutations together with ectopic expression studies argue for auto-catalytic degradation of YME1L1R149W.
source: However, the lack of wild-type YME1L1 in patient cells with homozygous YME1L1 mutations together with our ectopic expression studies argue for auto-catalytic degradation of YME1L1R149W.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the combination of patient cell data and experimental results.

claim: The dominant negative E381Q mutation in the ATPase domain of YME1L1 stabilizes the known YME1L1 substrate PRELID1.
source: However, by preventing the proteolytic activity of YME1L1 upon ectopic expression of the dominant-negative YME1L1E381Q, harboring a point mutation in the ATPase domain, we were able to stabilize not only the known YME1L1 substrate PRELID1 (Potting et al., 2013) but also observed accumulation of both the precursor and mature forms of YME1L1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: Western blot data in Figure 3A shows PRELID1 accumulation with E381Q mutation.

claim: Proteolysis by YME1L1 depends on its oligomerization.
source: As proteolysis by YME1L1 depends on its oligomerization, we examined in further experiments the assembly of YME1L1R149W expressed in HEK293 cells by sucrose gradient centrifugation (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about AAA protease function.
